The term OM has the same meaning as Medicare fee-for-service and the traditional Medicare program.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Employment level, 65 years and over, September 2026 — 11,654 thousands of people (-0.7% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: Fewer Americans over 65 had a job in September than a year ago
story_ideas.angle: A short read on the 11,654 thousand figure and its turn from +2.1% in August to -0.7%, written for people who built a retirement plan around working longer.
story_ideas.hook: The series that had been growing through the summer printed a year-over-year decline.
story_ideas.consumer: If your plan assumes income from work at 67 or 70, price out what one year without that paycheck does to your Social Security claiming date and your drawdown rate now, rather than after a layoff.
story_ideas.b2b: Employers courting older workers have a softening market to read: the 65-plus headcount fell year over year while health sector payrolls grew 2%.
story_ideas.why: An older worker who treats the paycheck as certain and loses it mid-year makes the claiming decision under pressure instead of on a schedule.
story_ideas.note: Monitored publishers did not match this item, and the series is national only, so the chart is the four care-sector lines against the 65-plus line.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Home health care services employment, September 2026 — 1,894.20 thousands of jobs (+4.4% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: Home health is still the fastest-hiring part of senior care, but it cooled this month
story_ideas.angle: A piece comparing the September +4.4% print against the August +5.0% print for families waiting on home care hours.
story_ideas.hook: Home health hiring is still the strongest in the sector while decelerating two months running.
story_ideas.consumer: If an agency told you there is no aide available for your hours, ask what its current open-position count is and whether it is placing new hires this month, because the national payroll is still growing.
story_ideas.b2b: Agencies are adding headcount into a flat overall labor market, which makes recruiting pitches that compete on wage rather than availability more exposed.
story_ideas.chart: The underlying file supports an original ranking or trend line.
story_ideas.competitive: Monitored trades cover this beat and have not written it.
story_ideas.why: A family that accepts a waitlist without asking can lose months of covered hours in a sector that is actively adding workers.
story_ideas.note: A confirmed gap among monitored publishers; pairs naturally with the hourly earnings series for a single chart.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Home health care services average hourly earnings, August 2026 — 28.14 dollars per hour (+2.4% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: $28.14 an hour is what home health work pays now
story_ideas.angle: What the August earnings print means for people hiring privately and for aides deciding whether to stay, with the 2.4% annual increase as the benchmark.
story_ideas.hook: Home health pay rose 2.4% over the year while assisted living pay rose 4.8%, the opposite of where the job growth went.
story_ideas.consumer: Before you agree to a private-pay rate, check it against the $28.14 national average so you know whether you are paying above or below the market and what an aide could get elsewhere.
story_ideas.b2b: Home health employers raising wages 2.4% are competing with congregate settings raising them 4.8%, which is a retention problem before it is a recruiting one.
story_ideas.why: A family paying blind can overpay an agency markup or underpay an aide who then leaves mid-arrangement.
story_ideas.note: Unmatched by monitored publishers; the August figure is the latest earnings print and will be superseded next month.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Nursing care facilities employment, September 2026 — 1,587.40 thousands of jobs (+1.9% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: Nursing home payrolls grew 1.9% this year. Ask what that looks like on your floor.
story_ideas.angle: A tour-day piece turning the 1,587.40 thousand national staffing figure into questions a family asks on a specific unit.
story_ideas.hook: Nursing facility employment grew for the year while the overall 65-plus workforce shrank.
story_ideas.consumer: On your next visit, ask for the unit's current staffing hours and how many positions are open, then set it against the fact that national nursing facility headcount is up 1.9% rather than accepting "nobody is hiring" as an answer.
story_ideas.b2b: A 1.9% national headcount gain is the number operators will be measured against in reimbursement and staffing arguments for fiscal 2027.
story_ideas.why: Families who cannot tell a staffing-constrained building from a sector-wide shortage cannot judge the one explanation they are given.
story_ideas.note: A confirmed gap; localizable only at the national level, so the comparison has to be building-level reporting against the national line.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Continuing care retirement communities and assisted living employment, September 2026 — 1,022.10 thousands of jobs (+0.8% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: Assisted living hiring has nearly stopped growing
story_ideas.angle: The 1,022.10 thousand figure and its 0.8% annual gain read against home health's 4.4%, for prospective residents comparing a community with staying home.
story_ideas.hook: Congregate senior living added staff at roughly a fifth of the rate home health did.
story_ideas.consumer: If you are weighing a community against home care, ask the community how its staff count today compares with a year ago, because nationally this is the slowest-growing care workforce of the three.
story_ideas.b2b: Flat headcount against 4.8% wage growth squeezes labor budgets just as fiscal 2027 plans take effect.
story_ideas.why: A resident who moves into a building that cannot grow its staff is making a years-long commitment on this month's staffing promise.
story_ideas.note: Lightly covered rather than a gap; the clean visual is the three care-sector growth rates side by side.

story_ideas.title: BLS: Assisted living and CCRC average hourly earnings, August 2026 — 25.89 dollars per hour (+4.8% year over year)
story_ideas.headline: Assisted living pay is rising faster than home health pay for the first time in these prints
story_ideas.angle: A wage comparison piece on $25.89 an hour rising 4.8% while home health's $28.14 rose 2.4%, for anyone choosing between the two settings or the two jobs.
story_ideas.hook: The lower-paying setting is raising wages twice as fast as the higher-paying one.
story_ideas.consumer: When a community explains a monthly fee increase by citing labor costs, you now have the number to ask about: average pay in this setting is $25.89 an hour, up 4.8% over the year.
story_ideas.b2b: Operators paying up 4.8% while adding only 0.8% headcount are buying retention, not capacity, and that distinction belongs in the rate conversation.
story_ideas.why: Residents facing fee increases deserve to know how much of the rise tracks a wage line they can look up.
story_ideas.note: Lightly covered; works as a two-line chart with the home health earnings series.

story_ideas.hook: Nebraska has early data on outcomes for people subject to the requirements before the national start date.

story_ideas.b2b: Providers serving dual eligibles and HCBS clients should map which of their enrollees fall under verification and where coverage losses would hit census.

story_ideas.b2b: HCBS providers and nonprofit operators have a direct census interest in whether the expanded eligibility rule is made permanent.

trends_raw: Volume is flat: 162 evidence candidates, the same count as the 10/01/26 run, but 33 of them are new, and the new material is concentrated in one place. The September BLS prints arrived and moved a number: employment of people 65 and over came in at 11,654 thousand, down 0.7% year over year, against the August print of 11,753 thousand that was up 2.1%, while home health (1,894.20 thousand, +4.4%), nursing care facilities (1,587.40 thousand, +1.9%) and assisted living and CCRCs (1,022.10 thousand, +0.8%) all kept growing. Medicare and Medicaid is the busiest beat again, 36 items from 7 sources, but at a cohesion of 0.05 it is not one story: a final GLOBE Model rule, a Medicare 101 chapter, four KFF work-requirements tracker pages, three Federal Register corrections and a refreshed supplier file share a tag and nothing else, and they should be worked as separate leads. Housing is one item quieter and has now carried two of the last three feature pitches, on 09/25/26 and 09/28/26, so this run moves off it. Two threads have gone unpitched for several runs: the palliative and hospice cluster, which at 0.204 is the most coherent in the run and holds the 09/30/26 hospice wage index correction, and the American Community Survey 2023 state aging and housing profile, which has appeared in evidence lists since 09/25/26 without ever leading a pitch despite carrying the only state-level counts in the corpus. Coverage posture: 52 confirmed gaps where monitored publishers work the beat and matched nothing, plus 73 items on beats no monitored publisher covers, which says nothing about whether anyone else has written them.
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** The September employment prints break the direction the older-worker series had been running in, and the care-sector series went the other way in the same month. BLS puts employment of people 65 years and over at 11,654 thousand in September 2026, down 0.7% year over year, after the August print of 11,753 thousand was up 2.1%. Over the same month home health care services employment reached 1,894.20 thousand jobs (+4.4%), nursing care facilities 1,587.40 thousand (+1.9%), and continuing care retirement communities and assisted living 1,022.10 thousand (+0.8%). KFF counts nearly 379,000 health sector jobs added over the past year, a 2% increase against 0.2% growth in other non-farm employment. The workforce cluster is the one beat this run where the sources actually land on the same subject rather than sharing a tag, and what they say together is that the fastest-hiring part of the economy is the part that cares for older adults, while the number of older adults holding a job is falling.

**Why it matters:** 11,654,000 people over 65 were working in September, roughly 99,000 fewer than the August print and down on the year, and that is the group for whom a job is the difference between drawing down savings and not. The jobs still being added are care jobs paying $28.14 an hour in home health (+2.4% year over year) and $25.89 in assisted living and CCRCs (+4.8%). An older worker who loses a position and looks at what is hiring is looking at direct care, at those wages, often for a neighbor their own age.

**Why pitch this now:** The September figures printed this month and will be overwritten by the October print; four of these series were first collected since the last pitch ran on 09/28/26, and the 65-and-over number moved from +2.1% to -0.7% between prints. Federal fiscal 2027 began 10/01/26, so operator budgets for the hiring year just took effect against these wage levels.

**Angle:** Whether the only labor market still expanding for older adults is the one that takes care of them, and what happens to the 65-and-over worker who was counted in August and not in September. Working title: "The Care Economy Is Hiring. Older Workers Are Not." For readers in their sixties and seventies who planned to work longer, and for the operators bidding for the same hours.

**Potential headlines:**
- Fewer Americans over 65 had a job in September than a year ago
- Care work kept hiring while the rest of the labor market stalled
- Home health added jobs at five times the rate assisted living did

**Potential outlets:**
- **Next Avenue** — covers work and caregiving for the same reader, who is both the person losing the job and the person hiring the aide
- **MarketWatch Retirement** — a monthly federal series reversing direction is exactly the economic read its retirement audience acts on
- **McKnight's Long-Term Care News** — nursing care facilities at 1,587.40 thousand jobs (+1.9%) is a staffing benchmark its operator readers measure themselves against
- **Senior Housing News** — +0.8% headcount growth with +4.8% wage growth in assisted living is a margin story its readers have to budget around
pitch_draft_raw: In September, BLS counted 11,654 thousand people aged 65 and over with a job, down 0.7% from a year earlier, after August's print of 11,753 thousand was up 2.1%. In the same month, the industries that care for that age group kept hiring: home health care services at 1,894.20 thousand jobs, up 4.4%; nursing care facilities up 1.9%; assisted living and continuing care communities up 0.8%. KFF counts nearly 379,000 health sector jobs added over the year, 2% growth against 0.2% everywhere else. I would like to write about 1,400 words on what that split means for someone who planned to work past 65: which jobs are actually being added, what they pay ($28.14 an hour in home health, $25.89 in assisted living and CCRCs), and why the openings an older job seeker finds are increasingly care work. It rests entirely on federal series readers can look up themselves, with a chart of the four lines over the past year. Next Avenue's readers sit on both sides of this at once.
pitch_ideas_raw:
**Fewer Americans over 65 had a job in September than a year ago**
*BLS: Employment level, 65 years and over, September 2026 — 11,654 thousands of people (-0.7% year over year)*  
- Angle: A short read on the 11,654 thousand figure and its turn from +2.1% in August to -0.7%, written for people who built a retirement plan around working longer.
- Hook: The series that had been growing through the summer printed a year-over-year decline.
- For readers: If your plan assumes income from work at 67 or 70, price out what one year without that paycheck does to your Social Security claiming date and your drawdown rate now, rather than after a layoff.
- For the trade: Employers courting older workers have a softening market to read: the 65-plus headcount fell year over year while health sector payrolls grew 2%.
- Why it matters: An older worker who treats the paycheck as certain and loses it mid-year makes the claiming decision under pressure instead of on a schedule.
- Also: Monitored publishers did not match this item, and the series is national only, so the chart is the four care-sector lines against the 65-plus line.
- Pitch to: Bankrate Retirement, GOBankingRates

**Home health is still the fastest-hiring part of senior care, but it cooled this month**
*BLS: Home health care services employment, September 2026 — 1,894.20 thousands of jobs (+4.4% year over year)*  
- Angle: A piece comparing the September +4.4% print against the August +5.0% print for families waiting on home care hours.
- Hook: Home health hiring is still the strongest in the sector while decelerating two months running.
- For readers: If an agency told you there is no aide available for your hours, ask what its current open-position count is and whether it is placing new hires this month, because the national payroll is still growing.
- For the trade: Agencies are adding headcount into a flat overall labor market, which makes recruiting pitches that compete on wage rather than availability more exposed.
- Why it matters: A family that accepts a waitlist without asking can lose months of covered hours in a sector that is actively adding workers.
- Also: A confirmed gap among monitored publishers; pairs naturally with the hourly earnings series for a single chart.
- Pitch to: Next Avenue, Caring.com

**$28.14 an hour is what home health work pays now**
*BLS: Home health care services average hourly earnings, August 2026 — 28.14 dollars per hour (+2.4% year over year)*  
- Angle: What the August earnings print means for people hiring privately and for aides deciding whether to stay, with the 2.4% annual increase as the benchmark.
- Hook: Home health pay rose 2.4% over the year while assisted living pay rose 4.8%, the opposite of where the job growth went.
- For readers: Before you agree to a private-pay rate, check it against the $28.14 national average so you know whether you are paying above or below the market and what an aide could get elsewhere.
- For the trade: Home health employers raising wages 2.4% are competing with congregate settings raising them 4.8%, which is a retention problem before it is a recruiting one.
- Why it matters: A family paying blind can overpay an agency markup or underpay an aide who then leaves mid-arrangement.
- Also: Unmatched by monitored publishers; the August figure is the latest earnings print and will be superseded next month.
- Pitch to: Workspan Daily, Next Avenue

**Nursing home payrolls grew 1.9% this year. Ask what that looks like on your floor.**
*BLS: Nursing care facilities employment, September 2026 — 1,587.40 thousands of jobs (+1.9% year over year)*  
- Angle: A tour-day piece turning the 1,587.40 thousand national staffing figure into questions a family asks on a specific unit.
- Hook: Nursing facility employment grew for the year while the overall 65-plus workforce shrank.
- For readers: On your next visit, ask for the unit's current staffing hours and how many positions are open, then set it against the fact that national nursing facility headcount is up 1.9% rather than accepting "nobody is hiring" as an answer.
- For the trade: A 1.9% national headcount gain is the number operators will be measured against in reimbursement and staffing arguments for fiscal 2027.
- Why it matters: Families who cannot tell a staffing-constrained building from a sector-wide shortage cannot judge the one explanation they are given.
- Also: A confirmed gap; localizable only at the national level, so the comparison has to be building-level reporting against the national line.
- Pitch to: Provider Magazine, Family Caregiver Alliance

**Assisted living hiring has nearly stopped growing**
*BLS: Continuing care retirement communities and assisted living employment, September 2026 — 1,022.10 thousands of jobs (+0.8% year over year)*  
- Angle: The 1,022.10 thousand figure and its 0.8% annual gain read against home health's 4.4%, for prospective residents comparing a community with staying home.
- Hook: Congregate senior living added staff at roughly a fifth of the rate home health did.
- For readers: If you are weighing a community against home care, ask the community how its staff count today compares with a year ago, because nationally this is the slowest-growing care workforce of the three.
- For the trade: Flat headcount against 4.8% wage growth squeezes labor budgets just as fiscal 2027 plans take effect.
- Why it matters: A resident who moves into a building that cannot grow its staff is making a years-long commitment on this month's staffing promise.
- Also: Lightly covered rather than a gap; the clean visual is the three care-sector growth rates side by side.
- Pitch to: McKnight's Senior Living, Senior Housing News

**Assisted living pay is rising faster than home health pay for the first time in these prints**
*BLS: Assisted living and CCRC average hourly earnings, August 2026 — 25.89 dollars per hour (+4.8% year over year)*  
- Angle: A wage comparison piece on $25.89 an hour rising 4.8% while home health's $28.14 rose 2.4%, for anyone choosing between the two settings or the two jobs.
- Hook: The lower-paying setting is raising wages twice as fast as the higher-paying one.
- For readers: When a community explains a monthly fee increase by citing labor costs, you now have the number to ask about: average pay in this setting is $25.89 an hour, up 4.8% over the year.
- For the trade: Operators paying up 4.8% while adding only 0.8% headcount are buying retention, not capacity, and that distinction belongs in the rate conversation.
- Why it matters: Residents facing fee increases deserve to know how much of the rise tracks a wage line they can look up.
- Also: Lightly covered; works as a two-line chart with the home health earnings series.
- Pitch to: McKnight's Senior Living, SeniorLiving.org

**Medicare just finalized a mandatory payment model for Part B drugs**
*Global Benchmark for Efficient Drug Pricing (GLOBE) Model*  
- Angle: A plain explanation of the final rule's alternative method for calculating Part B drug inflation rebate amounts, for people whose treatments are infused or administered in a clinic.
- Hook: The rule was published 10/02/26 and is mandatory under section 1115A of the Social Security Act rather than voluntary.
- For readers: If a drug you receive is billed under Part B rather than picked up at a pharmacy, keep this rule on your list of things to raise with the prescribing office, and ask whether your drug is among the separately payable products it covers.
- For the trade: A mandatory model changes rebate math for providers who buy and bill Part B drugs, so participation planning is not optional.
- Why it matters: Part B patients learn about payment model changes last, usually when a billing office explains them after the fact.
- Also: Published the day of this run and only lightly covered among monitored publishers; the rule text names the drug categories, so the reporting is in the specifics.
- Pitch to: Forbes Retirement, Fierce Healthcare

**CMS corrected the hospice payment rule for the fiscal year that just started**
*Medicare Program; FY 2027 Hospice Wage Index and Payment Rate Update and Hospice Quality Reporting Program Requirements; Correction*  
- Angle: A short piece on the 09/30/26 correction to the 08/03/26 hospice final rule and what the quality reporting requirements now say, for hospice boards and the families choosing among providers.
- Hook: The correction landed on the eve of the fiscal year the rule governs.
- For readers: When you are comparing hospices, ask each one which quality measures it reports to CMS and how it performed, since the reporting requirements for this fiscal year were just amended.
- For the trade: Hospice finance and compliance teams need to confirm which rates and reporting requirements the correction actually changed before billing against the August version.
- Why it matters: A family choosing hospice under time pressure relies on quality reporting that is only as current as the rule behind it.
- Also: A confirmed gap among monitored publishers, and the palliative and hospice cluster is the most internally coherent in this run.
- Pitch to: LeadingAge, Fierce Healthcare

**One state is already verifying Medicaid work requirements. Here is what the paperwork looks like.**
*Early Medicaid Work Requirement Insights From Nebraska*  
- Angle: A procedural read of the Nebraska verification process and its early outcome data, for older adults and caregivers whose coverage will be tested the same way.
- Hook: Nebraska has early data on outcomes for people subject to the requirements before the national start date.
- For readers: If you or the adult you care for is on Medicaid, find out now which verification documents your state will ask for and whether an exemption applies to you, rather than waiting for a renewal notice.
- For the trade: Providers serving dual eligibles and HCBS clients should map which of their enrollees fall under verification and where coverage losses would hit census.
- Why it matters: Coverage lost to a paperwork failure is as real as coverage lost to a rule change, and it falls on people who use the most care.
- Also: A confirmed gap; KFF's companion tracker dates the reconciliation law's work requirements to January 2027, which makes a state already running one the test case.
- Pitch to: Modern Healthcare, SeniorLiving.org

**The rule that keeps a spouse from going broke to get home care is temporary**
*Make the Spousal Impoverishment Protection for HCBS Permanent*  
- Angle: An explainer on the expanded Medicaid spousal impoverishment protection for home and community-based services and what its non-permanent status means for couples planning care at home.
- Hook: The protection that makes aging at home affordable for married couples rests on an expansion Congress has to keep renewing.
- For readers: If you are the healthy spouse of someone who needs home care, ask your state Medicaid agency in writing how your income and assets are counted under the current protection and what changes if the expansion lapses.
- For the trade: HCBS providers and nonprofit operators have a direct census interest in whether the expanded eligibility rule is made permanent.
- Why it matters: A couple that plans around a temporary eligibility rule can be moved from home care to institutional care by a rule they never saw expire.
- Also: Unmatched by monitored publishers; the long-term care cluster is one of the few in this run where the sources genuinely share a subject.
- Pitch to: Kiplinger, McKnight's Long-Term Care News

**What enhanced services did for veterans in permanent supportive housing**
*Veterans Support to Self-Reliance Pilot Program*  
- Angle: A read of the impact evaluation of California's initiative providing enhanced supportive services to veterans in permanent supportive housing, for anyone arguing that housing alone is not enough.
- Hook: An impact evaluation of a state pilot, published 09/30/26, tests whether added services change outcomes for people already housed.
- For readers: If you are an older veteran in supportive housing, or helping one, ask your housing provider which supportive services it actually delivers on site and which it only refers out.
- For the trade: Developers and operators building affordable senior and supportive housing can use an impact evaluation to argue the services budget, not just the capital stack.
- Why it matters: Residents of supportive housing lose the benefit the model is built on when the services half of it is unfunded.
- Also: A confirmed gap among monitored publishers; California-specific, which makes it a template story other states can be measured against.
- Pitch to: Senior Housing News, Next Avenue
